visible.summary:
North Ossetia–Alania is included in the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its general finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia. Western travel advisories name the republic within the broader Caucasus don't-travel area. The enforcement logic is the same as neighbouring republics: family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return without legal process.

No Chechnya-scale secret-prison infrastructure or explicit special-permission entry requirement is documented for North Ossetia specifically. Approximately 0.07 below national (0.12). Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia in the broader North Caucasus bloc. Well above the central-Russian oblasts, which inherit the national score with no sub-national deviation.
visible.tangentialFactors: The informal-enforcement pattern documented for the zone - round-ups, detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process - was first recorded against gay men and LGBTIQ+ people generally rather than trans people specifically; the same security-and-custom logic operates on any discovered queer visitor, trans or not.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The Western don't-travel designation for the North Caucasus zone is driven largely by general armed-conflict and security risk that affects all travellers; the trans-relevant content is the LGBT-specific exception drawn by the UK Home Office note, not the blanket advisory level.

sources.claim: Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; year-on-year deterioration from an on-the-ground defender in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): singles out the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation → 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment.

Wikipedia (LGBTQ rights in Russia), the federal framework applying in North Ossetia–Alania: in November 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as an extremist group, making participation in LGBT activism illegal. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition, and the federal 'propaganda' law of 2013 was expanded in December 2022 to apply to people of all ages and to materials that make minors interested in gender transition; new laws effective 1 July 2023 effectively reclassify homosexuality as a mental illness. Confirms that visible LGBT activity a visitor brings into the republic sits entirely outside federal legal protection.

visible.summary:
Stavropol Krai is named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia) and is included in the North Caucasus zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN as the exception to Russia's general risk picture. The dossier specifically identifies the south-eastern part bordering Chechnya as subject to the same security-and-custom enforcement logic. However, Stavropol is a krai, not a republic, and the extreme documented violence (secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription) is Chechen-specific rather than krai-wide.

For a visitor, the special-permission regime itself restricts movement and independent oversight, and the south-eastern areas adjacent to Chechnya share the localised security culture. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.05 below. Above the core North Caucasus republics (Dagestan, Ingushetia at 0.04; Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, North Ossetia at 0.05) because the extreme evidence is geographically limited to the Chechnya border zone within a large multi-ethnic krai, and no independent republic-level security apparatus analogous to Kadyrov's exists.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Caucasus-zone enforcement logic the dossier documents applies to LGBTIQ+ people broadly; the special-permission and checkpoint culture is not trans-status-specific.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The special-permission requirement Canada identifies for this krai applies to all foreign travellers regardless of personal characteristic - a movement-control measure whose trans-relevant content is only what it signals about the security apparatus near the Chechnya border; the advisory zone itself reflects general insecurity.

sources.claim: Global Affairs Canada Russia advisory (retrieved): avoid-all-travel; frequent terrorist attacks named for Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and the Stavropol region; MOI special permission required to enter certain areas (list: Kabardino-Balkaria incl. Elbrus, Karachai-Cherkessia, North Ossetia); 2SLGBTQI+ persons/ally families attacked, harassed and abused; since Jan 2024 advocacy organisations treated as 'extremist'; foreigner surveillance warned.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): singles out the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation → 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment.

Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; year-on-year deterioration from an on-the-ground defender in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

visible.summary:
Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.
visible.tangentialFactors: The extremism-designation prosecutions centred on Moscow target organisers and LGBT-facing venues broadly, not only trans people - the general anti-LGBT enforcement climate is part of what a trans-presenting visitor is exposed to.
visible.localsOnly: The medical and bureaucratic gatekeeping the 2023 federal transition ban concentrates here bears on residents navigating transition paperwork and care; a visitor's exposure is enforcement-side (venue raids, document and registration checks, the propaganda-law detention and deportation risk).
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The blanket don't-travel levels (State Department, FCDO) reflect wrongful-detention and war risk for all travellers; they are not trans-specific evidence, though the propaganda-law detention rule embedded in them is.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (paywall shell); the underlying Moscow Times 2025 survey of persecution is titled around 'arrests, club raids and extremism charges' defining LGBTQ life in Russia in 2025, and records that Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (paywall shell); the underlying Moscow Times report (February 2025) covered Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation - an organising case, following a court ruling in Siberia reported January 2025.

Wikipedia's Russia country overview records the federal framework a Moscow visitor stands under: the Supreme Court in November 2023 declared the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and on 22 March 2024 it was formally added to the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations, a designation the page says has led to arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges. The page also records the July 2023 federal law banning gender transition outright - both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition - plus Moscow-specific facts: Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, and in 2011 the head of the Moscow Registry Office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail."

visible.summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in Russia (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a Siberian court in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.
visible.tangentialFactors: The case is prosecuted as membership of the 'international LGBT movement' as such - the precedent it sets covers venues serving gay men and LGBT people generally as much as trans people, and forms part of the enforcement backdrop any queer visitor shares.

sources.claim: OVD-Info (10 Jul 2025): Orenburg's Central District Court registered materials in Russia's first criminal case under the Supreme Court's 'international LGBT movement' extremism ban - Pose club staff, case opened Mar 2024, sent to court 9 Jul 2025.

Novaya Gazeta Europe (29 Jun 2026): Orenburg region Pose bar owner Vyacheslav Khasanov sentenced to 7 years plus 1m rubles forfeiture, manager Diana Kamilyanova to 6 years 3 months, art director Alexander Klimov to 2 years 3 months - Russia's first known 'LGBT extremism' convictions, concluded in the region.

visible.summary:
Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: only 157 people used the Gender Identity Law (21.120) for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), La Araucanía is 0.01 higher: Tarapacá carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas Araucanía's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because Araucanía's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising region with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.
visible.tangentialFactors: The +150 % rise counts discrimination complaints on sexual orientation together with gender expression and identity; the homophobic (LGB) component drives much of the increase but shapes the same climate of hostility a trans visitor would meet.
visible.localsOnly: The 157-rectification figure measures residents' use of the civil-registry procedure under Law 21.120; it signals community size and institutional presence, not a condition a short-term visitor encounters.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Parts of La Araucanía sit within a prolonged Mapuche land-and-security conflict that affects all travellers and is not trans-specific; the finding above concerns the trajectory of LGBTIQ+ complaints, not the conflict itself.

sources.claim: Araucanía Noticias (24 Mar 2026): Movilh's XXIV annual report names La Araucanía the region where recorded homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — +150% year-on-year. The same report put the national total at a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1% on 2024), with 2025 alone accounting for 23% of all cases in the 24-year series.

Movilh XXIV annual report (Mar 2026, 2025 data): La Araucanía accounted for 1.96% of the national case total while ranking first in year-on-year growth (+150%) — the report's own regional tables are the dataset basis for both the rise and share claims in this record; the region-specific news article does not carry the share figure (rule 5).

visible.summary:
Ñuble registered a +300 % increase in recorded homo/transphobic cases in 2024, the sharpest percentage rise of any Chilean region, though from an extremely small base: Ñuble held only 1.44 % of the national case total. La Discusión's reporting of two historic gender-identity rectification cases in Ñuble illustrates how minimal the formal trans presence is in the region. The statistical alarm is real — the fastest percentage growth in the country — but the absolute numbers remain marginal, and no region-specific legal finding, institutional incident, or enforcement failure was identified in the dossier beyond the case-volume trend. A 2026 follow-up in the same paper reports homo/transphobic attacks rising a further 16.6 % in Ñuble in 2025.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.05 deviation, driven entirely by the rate-of-change signal. Compared with Bío-Bío (0.62), which is 0.05 lower, Ñuble lacks the hospital bed-placement and diversity-office-dismantling findings that give Bío-Bío a concrete traveler-facing institutional failure. Ñuble's evidence is statistical trajectory without a named incident. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Ñuble is 0.02 higher: Araucanía's +150 % is in the most recent year (2025) and is accompanied by the lowest gender-identity-law uptake of any region (157 in three years), painting a more sustained picture of emerging hostility with no institutional counterweight.
visible.tangentialFactors: Ñuble's case figures are Movilh's combined homo/transphobia series — the +300 % 2024 surge and the 2025 +16.6 % attack rise include homophobic (LGB) cases and do not isolate trans-specific events.
visible.localsOnly: The rectification cases are civil-registry matters for residents (birth-certificate/name-marker change under the national gender-identity law, and the waitlist for state-transition healthcare one interviewee describes); they evidence a tiny local trans population rather than visitor-facing services.

sources.claim: Movilh Chile (18 Mar 2025): the annual human-rights report (2024 data) records 2,847 documented homo/transphobic abuses nationwide, +78.7% year-on-year, 23.5% of all cases since the series began — and Ñuble tops the regional rise table at +300% from a 1.44% share of the national total, the sharpest percentage increase of any Chilean region.

La Discusión (11 Jul 2026): 12,669 people have changed their legal name and sex nationally since the Gender Identity Law (21.120) took effect (through 2025); the article profiles two historic rectification cases in Ñuble — concrete evidence of how minimal formal trans presence remains in the region.
